title: Polynomial-time linear convergence for geodesically convex optimization
formal: In the geometric arithmetic model below, is there a deterministic first-order algorithm and absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) that minimize every Lipschitz geodesically convex function on a strongly geodesically convex ball in a complete Riemannian manifold, using at most \(C(d+\zeta)^a\lceil\log(2/\varepsilon)\rceil\) objective-oracle queries and at most \(C(d+\zeta)^b\) additional operations between consecutive queries? Here \(d\) is the manifold dimension, \(\zeta=r\sqrt K/\tanh(r\sqrt K)\), with value one at \(K=0\), and the required additive objective error is \(\varepsilon Lr\). The same polynomial overhead bound applies before the first query and after the last.
why: Euclidean cutting-plane methods show that high accuracy need not require a polynomial number of inverse-accuracy steps. Extending that efficiency to geodesic convexity would provide a general computational foundation for optimization on curved spaces, including matrix geometries used in scaling and statistical models.
status_note: The joint query-and-computation question is open in the 2023 source. A bounded review on 13 September 2026 did not find a resolution for the full geodesically convex class. The computational oracle convention is an explicit editorial specification, not a claim that all manifolds admit efficient finite-precision geometric implementations.

progress.text: Criscitiello, Martínez-Rubio and Boumal pose the full joint-resource question and prove a constant-curvature result with a squared logarithm in inverse accuracy.
Criscitiello and Kim develop a theory and algorithms for the more restrictive horospherically convex setting.

sentences: Geodesically convex optimization replaces straight segments with shortest paths on a Riemannian manifold.
The question asks for a deterministic first-order algorithm with query complexity polynomial in dimension and logarithmic in inverse accuracy.
It also requires polynomial arithmetic work per query, so a powerful but computationally intractable geometric oracle would not suffice.
The source develops an ellipsoid-like approach for constant-curvature spaces and identifies obstacles on more general manifolds.
A solution would extend the efficient precision dependence of Euclidean convex optimization to curved spaces while respecting the cost of manipulating their geometry.

definitions: The input consists of a complete connected smooth \(d\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), \(d\geq1\), a reference point \(x_0\), a radius \(r>0\), a Lipschitz bound \(L>0\), a sectional-curvature bound \(K\geq0\), and real \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\). All sectional curvatures lie in \([-K,K]\). The distance \(\operatorname{dist}\) is the infimum of lengths of connecting curves in the given Riemannian metric. The closed ball \(D=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x_0,x)\leq r\}\) is promised strongly geodesically convex: every two points of \(D\) have a unique minimizing geodesic in \(\mathcal M\), and its whole segment lies in \(D\). If \(\gamma\) is such a segment parametrized on \([0,1]\) at constant speed, the unknown function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(f(\gamma(t))\leq(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+tf(\gamma(1))\), and \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\). A function query at \(x\in D\) returns \(f(x)\) exactly and any tangent vector \(g\in T_x\mathcal M\) satisfying \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rangle_x\) for every \(y\in D\); correctness is required for every valid sequence of returned subgradients. Here \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) is the initial velocity at time zero of the unit-time minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\). Only functions and subgradient oracles meeting these conditions are inputs. The output must be a point \(\widehat x\in D\) with \(f(\widehat x)-\min_D f\leq\varepsilon Lr\). Completeness makes the closed bounded ball compact, so this minimum exists. The algorithm has no access to a formula for \(f\). For computational access to geometry, points and tangent vectors are exact typed objects supplied by a geometric oracle; the input includes an orthonormal basis of \(T_{x_0}\mathcal M\). The available geometric operations are: distance between points; inner product of two vectors in one tangent space; linear combination of such vectors; \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)\), the time-one point of the geodesic with initial velocity \(v\); \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) for \(x,y\in D\); and parallel transport of a tangent vector along the explicitly specified geodesic \(t\mapsto\operatorname{Exp}_x(tv)\), \(0\leq t\leq1\). Each such operation is charged \((d+1)^3\) units, irrespective of point or vector magnitude. Object storage and access cost one unit; objects cannot be inspected except by these operations. Exact real scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root on nonnegative arguments, exponential, logarithm on positive arguments, comparisons and integer indexing operations each cost one unit. There is no floor or extraction of bits from a real register. All computation, including geometric operations, is charged apart from the separately counted function queries. One uniform finite program must work for every admissible manifold, basis, oracle and parameter tuple. There is no randomization, integral oracle, convex-hull oracle or free optimization subroutine.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the required uniform objective accuracy, logarithmic query dependence on inverse accuracy, and polynomial overhead independent of inverse accuracy, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated access model. A query bound with an uncomputable geometric step, a theorem only for a particular manifold, or an additional logarithmic factor in the query count does not meet the target. A negative result must allow the full list of geometric primitives provided here.

context_blocks.text: This retains the manifold, curvature, ball and objective quantifiers of the source’s Open Question 1. The source leaves the computational representation of a general manifold implicit. The listed exact geometric primitives and their costs are an explicit editorial choice making its arithmetic-overhead requirement testable. A result in this model is not automatically a polynomial bit-complexity result for an arbitrary encoded metric.

The parameter \(\zeta\) is comparable within universal constants to \(1+r\sqrt K\). It allows dependence on the curvature scale and radius. The source explains that curvature dependence cannot generally be removed, even though logarithmic dependence on inverse accuracy remains the requested target.

The source distinguishes methods with good query complexity but expensive geometric work from subgradient methods with cheap steps but slower precision dependence. Thus proving either resource guarantee separately does not settle the joint question.

For constant-curvature spaces the source gives an ellipsoid-like method with \(O(\zeta d^2\log^2(1/\varepsilon))\) queries and polynomial per-query work. This is a substantial partial result, but its extra logarithm and restricted geometry are both relevant to the full statement.

Positive definite matrices with the affine-invariant Riemannian metric are an important nonconstant-curvature example discussed by the source. Boumal’s textbook gives explicit distance, exponential and logarithmic maps for that geometry. These differ from the log-Euclidean metric, under which a coordinate logarithm makes convexity Euclidean.

Criscitiello and Kim’s 2025 work develops algorithms for horospherical convexity, a stronger geometric notion with additional structure. It does not by itself supply the required method for every geodesically convex objective in this question.
